::: {.callout-note}
## This section is optional

Everything here goes beyond what we covered live. In the workshop, you
organized raw vs. trimmed FastQC outputs by writing two separate processes
(`fastqc_raw` and `fastqc_trimmed`). That solution works and uses nothing
beyond what you already know — this page is for anyone curious about how a
more experienced Nextflow user might solve the same problem with fewer
lines of duplicated code.
:::

## Recap: the workshop solution

In Day 1, you had two processes with identical bodies, differing only in
`publishDir`:

```groovy
process fastqc_raw {
    module 'fastqc/0.12.1'
    stageInMode 'copy'
    publishDir 'results/qc_raw', mode: 'copy'

    input:
    path reads

    output:
    path "*_fastqc.{html,zip}"

    script:
    """
    fastqc -t 4 ${reads}
    """
}

process fastqc_trimmed {
    module 'fastqc/0.12.1'
    stageInMode 'copy'
    publishDir 'results/qc_trimmed', mode: 'copy'

    input:
    path reads

    output:
    path "*_fastqc.{html,zip}"

    script:
    """
    fastqc -t 4 ${reads}
    """
}
```

This was the right call for the workshop: it needed nothing you hadn't
already learned. But it does mean maintaining two copies of the same
logic — if you ever changed the FastQC command, you'd need to change it in
two places. Below are two ways to avoid that duplication.

## Option A: tag, merge, and let `publishDir` branch at runtime

Instead of two processes, you can carry a small "which stage is this"
label alongside each file through the channel, merge both stages into one
channel, and let a single process branch its output directory based on
that label.

This uses three ideas that weren't covered in the workshop:

- **`.map()` to attach a tag** to each file as it enters the channel
- **`.mix()` to merge two channels** into one, so a single process call can
  handle both stages
- **A dynamic `publishDir`** — instead of a fixed string, `publishDir` can
  take a closure that's evaluated separately for each task

```groovy
process fastqc {
    module 'fastqc/0.12.1'
    stageInMode 'copy'
    publishDir { "results/qc_${stage}" }, mode: 'copy'

    input:
    tuple val(stage), path(reads)

    output:
    path "*_fastqc.{html,zip}"

    script:
    """
    fastqc -t 4 ${reads}
    """
}

workflow {
    main:
    reads_ch = Channel.fromPath('data/sample_*_*.fastq')

    raw_tagged     = reads_ch.map { file -> tuple('raw', file) }
    trimmed_tagged = trim(reads_ch).map { file -> tuple('trimmed', file) }

    fastqc(raw_tagged.mix(trimmed_tagged))
}
```

One process, called once. The `{ "results/qc_${stage}" }` syntax is a
closure — Nextflow evaluates it separately for every task, using that
task's own `stage` value, rather than treating `publishDir` as one fixed
path shared by every task.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Why not teach this in the workshop?

It stacks three unfamiliar ideas — tagging, merging, and dynamic
directories — into a single example. Any one of them on its own is a
reasonable next step after Day 1; all three at once is a lot to absorb in
a stretch task with no lecture time behind it. This page exists so you can
come back to it once the individual pieces feel more familiar.
:::

## Option B: one process body, reused under two names

Nextflow has a mechanism for exactly this situation: pulling a process out
into its own file (a *module*) and importing it more than once under
different aliases. This is the direction Day 2's `include` syntax
material is building toward, so if you've made it that far, this will look
familiar.

`modules/fastqc.nf`:

```groovy
process fastqc {
    module 'fastqc/0.12.1'
    stageInMode 'copy'

    input:
    path reads

    output:
    path "*_fastqc.{html,zip}"

    script:
    """
    fastqc -t 4 ${reads}
    """
}
```

Main workflow file:

```groovy
include { fastqc as fastqc_raw     } from './modules/fastqc.nf'
include { fastqc as fastqc_trimmed } from './modules/fastqc.nf'

workflow {
    main:
    reads_ch = Channel.fromPath('data/sample_*_*.fastq')

    fastqc_raw(reads_ch)
    trim(reads_ch)
    fastqc_trimmed(trim.out)
}
```

The process body lives in exactly one place. Each `include` line gives it
a different name, so you can call it twice in the same workflow — solving
the "process already used" error from a different angle than either the
workshop fix or Option A.
